paragraphs.heading: Sorting crystals by symmetry
paragraphs.text: A crystal system, in crystallography, is a set of point groups. A point group is a group of geometric symmetries that has at least one fixed point. Loosely speaking, two crystals share a crystal system when their symmetries are similar, though there are many exceptions.

paragraphs.heading: Three schemes that get mixed up
paragraphs.text: Crystals can be classified in three ways: by lattice system, by crystal system and by crystal family. A lattice system is a set of Bravais lattices, and a Bravais lattice is an infinite array of discrete points. What gets sorted are space groups, which are symmetry groups of a configuration in space. A space group's point group decides its crystal system, and its Bravais lattice decides its lattice system. When several crystal systems have space groups assigned to one common lattice system, they are combined into a crystal family. The schemes are often confused, since people sometimes say "crystal system" when they mean a lattice system or a crystal family.

paragraphs.heading: Counting them
paragraphs.text: In two-dimensional space the three schemes come out the same, and the crystal families number four: oblique, rectangular, square and hexagonal. In three-dimensional space the count is 7 crystal systems, 7 lattice systems and 6 crystal families. Five crystal systems are essentially the same as five lattice systems: triclinic, monoclinic, orthorhombic, tetragonal and cubic. Go up to four-dimensional space and the totals become 33 crystal systems, 33 lattice systems and 23 crystal families.

paragraphs.heading: The trigonal and hexagonal tangle
paragraphs.text: The crystal systems called hexagonal and trigonal are not the same as the lattice systems called hexagonal and rhombohedral. Three dimensions have 32 crystallographic point groups, and most of them are assigned to just one lattice system. But for 5 point groups, 7 of the corresponding space groups fall in the rhombohedral lattice system and 18 fall in the hexagonal lattice system. Those 5 point groups are assigned to the trigonal crystal system. People often mix up the trigonal crystal system with the rhombohedral lattice system, and no "trigonal" lattice system exists.

paragraphs.heading: Down to 14 lattices
paragraphs.text: There are seven kinds of lattice system, and each kind has four kinds of centering: primitive, base-centered, body-centered and face-centered. Not every combination is unique, though. Some combinations are equivalent to others, and some are not possible for reasons of symmetry. This cuts the number of unique lattices down to 14, the 14 Bravais lattices.

paragraphs.heading: Two combinations that drop out
paragraphs.text: A base-centered cubic lattice is absent. If centering points are placed on only a single pair of opposite faces, the threefold rotation axes that define the cubic crystal system are removed, and the lattice that results is not cubic but a body-centered tetragonal lattice whose unit cell is smaller. A face-centered tetragonal lattice is redundant. Its array of points forms a body-centered tetragonal lattice that is equivalent, turned 45° around the c-axis, with the unit cell volume halved.
